newsitem.title: USA: Labor health care funds sue tobacco companies.
newsitem.headline: Labor health care funds sue tobacco companies.

text.p: A new front has been opened in the tobacco wars with labour union health care funds the latest groups to seek compensation for the costs of treating sick smokers.

A class-action lawsuit, filed late last week in U.S. District Court in Seattle, charges major tobacco companies with violating fraud and racketeering laws and demands unspecified restitution and punitive damages.
The lawsuit is the latest to be filed against an industry besieged by claims for damages from states, municipalities, private insurers and hundreds of individuals.

Like similar lawsuits filed by 22 states, the 110-page complaint filed by two Seattle-based labour union trust funds alleges a "conspiracy" among major tobacco companies to withhold information about the health effects of cigarettes and to supress development of potentially safer devices.

As a result of the alleged conspiracy and other factors, including advertising targeted at blue-collar workers, the funds contend they incurred "vastly" higher costs and lost premiums due to the premature deaths of workers.

In addition to monetary damages, the funds are asking the court to order the tobacco companies to stop marketing cigarettes with raised or manipulated nicotine levels and to stop targeting blue-collar workers and minors in advertising.
The plaintiffs in the case are the Northwest-Labourers Health & Security Trust Fund and the Carpenters Health and Security Trust of Western Washington.
Their attorney, George Kargianis, said he would ask the court to certify the case as a class action covering 100 funds representing hundreds of thousands of people in Washington, Oregon and Idaho.
He said lawyers were still calculating potential damages in the case but called them "substantial."

Defendants include Philip Morris Cos. Inc., R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.; and five other tobacco companies as well as the Tobacco Institute and other industry groups and representatives.

Notably absent from the lawsuit was Liggett Group, the smallest of the major U.S. tobacco companies, which settled this year with the 22 states, admitting nicotine is addictive and agreeing to turn over sensitive documents.
Liggett is a unit of Brooke Group Ltd.
